How to use this primer

This booklet teaches solar thermal engineering from zero, in the order the exam needs it. Read it once before the Complete Solutions. Each section has a green core idea box (learn this first), the key terms, the formulas with every symbol and unit, and a short worked example. Section 2 is a maths refresher: most marks lost in this course come from degree/radian mix-ups, wrong signs of angles, and kelvin vs Celsius in radiation formulas.

The pass set (from the Question Map): Section A topics A1 (sun angles), A2 (solar radiation and instruments), A3 (radiation laws) and A5 (collectors); Section B topics B2 (concentrators), B3 (water heating and storage) and B4 (drying, stills, cooling, power). These cover Q1, Q2, Q4, Q6, Q7 and Q8, enough for three full questions in each section. A4 (view factors) and B1 (collector losses and UL) are the next to add.

The whole course on one page

Read the map left to right: first find where the sun is and how much radiation reaches a surface; then learn the physics of radiation (how surfaces absorb, emit and exchange it); finally see how collectors turn it into heat and how that heat is used (hot water, drying, distillation, cooling, electricity).

Maths and units refresher

Set your calculator to degrees for all sun-angle work. Use kelvin in every T4 and in Planck’s law. Keep 4 significant figures in intermediate steps.

Trigonometry you need

  • sin, cos, tan of negative angles: sin(−x) = −sin x, cos(−x) = cos x, tan(−x) = −tan x. Southern declination and morning hour angles are negative.
  • Inverse: if cosωs = 0.159 then ωs = cos−1(0.159) = 80.85°.
  • Radians: π rad = 180°; in formulas with ωs(π/180) the angle is converted to radians.
  • Small angles: sinθ ≈ θ (rad) when θ < 1°; sin(0.265°) = 0.004625.

Day number n and time

Monthn for day iMonthn for day i
JaniJul181 + i
Feb31 + iAug212 + i
Mar59 + iSep243 + i
Apr90 + iOct273 + i
May120 + iNov304 + i
Jun151 + iDec334 + i

1 hour = 15° of hour angle; 1° of longitude = 4 minutes of time. Irradiance (W/m2) × time (s) = irradiation (J/m2); 1 MJ/m2 in one hour = 277.8 W/m2.

Hyperbolic functions and exponentials

  • tanh x = (ex − e−x)/(ex + e−x); for small x, tanh x ≈ x, so the fin efficiency tanh x/x → 1.
  • 1 − e−x ≈ x − x2/2 for small x; F″ = (1/x)(1 − e−x) ≈ 1 − x/2.
  • Fourth powers: 6004 = 1.296×1011, σ6004 = 7348 W/m2; σ10004 = 56,700 W/m2.

Iteration

Some problems (top loss coefficient) need an unknown temperature to find the coefficients that give that temperature. Guess, compute, update, repeat until two answers agree (usually 2-3 rounds).

The sun and its angles (A1)

The sun’s direction at any moment is fixed by three things: where you are (latitude φ), which day it is (declination δ) and what time it is (hour angle ω). From these, the zenith angle θz (how high the sun is) and, for a tilted surface, the angle of incidence θ follow by spherical trigonometry.

cosθz = cosφ cosδ cosω + sinφ sinδ; cosωs = −tanφ tanδ; N = 2ωs/15

SymbolMeaningUnit
φlatitude, + northdeg
δdeclinationdeg
ωhour angle, 15°/h, morning −deg
θz, αszenith angle, altitude angle = 90 − θzdeg
γs, γsolar and surface azimuth, 0 = south, west +deg
βsurface slopedeg
nday of the year–
Nday lengthh

Example: Khulna (φ = 22.8°) on January 18: δ = −20.73°, cosωs = 0.159, ωs = 80.85°, N = 10.78 h.

Solar radiation at the ground (A2)

Outside the atmosphere, 1367 W/m2 arrives as a parallel beam. At the ground it is split into beam and diffuse parts; the clearer the sky (higher KT), the more is beam. A tilted surface gets beam (times Rb), sky diffuse and ground-reflected radiation.

IT = IbRb + Id(1 + cosβ)/2 + Iρg(1 − cosβ)/2

SymbolMeaningUnit
Gscsolar constant 1367W/m2
H, Hodaily radiation at ground, extraterrestrialMJ/m2
KTclearness index H/Ho–
Ib, Idbeam, diffuse (horizontal)W/m2 or MJ/m2h
Rbgeometric factor cosθ/cosθz–
ρgground reflectance (albedo, ~0.2)–

Example: Ib = 400, Id = 150 W/m2, Rb = 1.2, β = 25°, ρg = 0.2: IT = 480 + 143.0 + 5.2 = 628 W/m2.

Radiation physics (A3, A4)

Every surface emits εσT4. A blackbody (ε = 1) is the ideal. Hot sources emit short waves, warm plates long waves (Wien). A good absorber is a good emitter at the same wavelength (Kirchhoff). Between surfaces, the exchange depends on the view factor and is solved with a resistance network.

SymbolMeaningUnit
σStefan-Boltzmann constant 5.67×10−8W/m2K4
Ebblackbody emissive power σT4W/m2
Iintensity (per steradian)W/m2sr
ε, α, ρ, τemissivity, absorptivity, reflectivity, transmissivity–
J, Gradiosity, irradiationW/m2
Fijview factor i to j–
λwavelengthμm

Example: plates at 900 K (ε 0.7) and 500 K (ε 0.5): q = σ(9004 − 5004)/(1/0.7 + 1/0.5 − 1) = 13.9 kW/m2.

Solar collectors and their performance (A5, B1)

A flat plate collector is a black plate with tubes, under glass, in an insulated box. It absorbs S = (τα)I and loses UL(Tp − Ta); the difference is the useful heat. Written with the inlet temperature: Qu = AcFR[S − UL(Ti − Ta)]. An evacuated tube removes most of the loss.

SymbolMeaningUnit
Accollector aream2
Sabsorbed solar (τα)ITW/m2
UL, Ut, Ub, Ueoverall, top, bottom, edge loss coefficientsW/m2K
F′, FR, F″efficiency factor, heat removal factor, flow factor–
Ffin efficiency–
W, D, Ditube spacing, outer and inner diameterm
hfifluid-side heat transfer coefficientW/m2K
ṁ, cpmass flow, specific heatkg/s, J/kg K
Ti, To, Ta, Tpinlet, outlet, ambient, plate°C

Example: 4 m2, FR = 0.868, S = 640 W/m2, UL = 6.9, Ti − Ta = 5: Qu = 4 × 0.868 × (640 − 34.5) = 2.10 kW; η = 2102/3200 = 66%.

Concentrating collectors (B2)

A mirror or lens of aperture Aa focuses beam radiation onto a small receiver Ar. The concentration ratio C = Aa/Ar sets how hot the receiver can get; its upper limit 1/sin2θs ≈ 46,747 comes from the sun’s finite size and the second law. Concentrators must track the sun.

SymbolMeaningUnit
Cconcentration ratio Aa/Ar–
2θcacceptance angledeg
θshalf-angle of the sun ≈ 0.265°deg
γintercept factor–

Example: a trough with 5 m aperture width and a 70 mm receiver tube (circumference 0.22 m): C = 5/0.22 ≈ 23.

Water heating, storage and other uses (B3, B4)

Hot water rises: a tank above the collector gives free circulation (thermosiphon); otherwise a pump with a differential controller is used. A storage tank is followed hour by hour with an energy balance. Other uses: dryers (warm air), stills (evaporate and condense), desiccant/absorption cooling, and concentrators that drive turbines.

Ts+ = Ts + [Qu − L − UA(Ts − Ta)Δt]/(mcp); qew = 0.016273hcw(Pw − Pg)

SymbolMeaningUnit
Qu, Luseful gain and load in one hourMJ
UAtank loss coefficient × areaW/K
mmass of water in the tankkg
hcwconvective coefficient water-glassW/m2K
Pw, Pgvapour pressure at water and glass temperaturePa
λlatent heat of evaporationJ/kg

Example: 500 kg tank at 45 °C, room 20 °C, UA = 12 W/K, no sun, load 12 MJ: loss = 12 × 3600 × 25 = 1.08 MJ; T = 45 − 13.08/2.09 = 38.7 °C after one hour.
